title: Homo Memorabiliaxis: Souvenirs and the Evolution of Autobiographical Memory and Self
abstract: ABSTRACTHumans routinely keep souvenirs objects retained for the memories they evoke, yet the evolutionary and cognitive consequences of mnemonic collecting remain unclear. Existing discussions of curated objects concentrate on later prehistory and modern humans and view such objects at the social level, as carriers of shared cultural meaning or as markers of status. Here, we address an earlier time period and locate the phenomenon at the personal rather than the social level. By integrating archaeology with theories of extended memory and niche construction, we synthesize evidence consistent with systematic curation of items beyond purely utilitarian needs from the terminal Lower Palaeolithic (~500 kya) onward, including transported distinctive stones, fossils, and the prolonged retention of patinated “old” stone tools whose earlier surfaces were deliberately preserved. We propose that curated keepsakes functioned as portable external memory devices. Beyond cueing recall, they may have helped authenticate self‐relevant past events by providing durable material traces that support source monitoring—distinguishing experienced from imagined events. As such practices became routine, they could have created a “souvenir niche” in which individuals who better integrated internal recollection with external tokens gained fitness benefits. The token's reference is personal, but its consequences can be social, supporting tasks like tracking alliances, reciprocity, and place‐based obligations. These benefits may have strengthened selection on neural systems facilitating the development of autobiographical memory and sense of self via gene–culture coevolution. We outline archaeological, developmental, and experimental predictions that distinguish this mnemonic‐authentication account from aesthetic or economic explanations and suggest approaches for testing them. Viewing curated objects as memory technology links early material culture to the evolutionary shaping of human autobiographical memory.

section: Hypothesis for the Evolutionary Role of Souvenirs
paragraphs.text: Humans collect and keep objects to remember. We collect stones from a place we may never see again, shells from a visit at the beach we want to recall, or artefacts passed down by loved ones. Have humans always been collectors and keepers? Since the emergence of the genus Homo some 2.5 million years ago, archaeological evidence indicates that early humans, like other great apes, acquired and transported resources needed for survival and reproduction, including fruits, nuts, and scavenged carcasses. Unlike most other animals, humans also systematically collected stones. Having no claws or sharp teeth, early humans used stone tools to make a living, and the procedures developed for stone tool production are the earliest evidence of human technology [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].

section: Hypothesis for the Evolutionary Role of Souvenirs
paragraphs.text: But what about collecting items for sentimental, mnemonic, or emotional reasons, a pattern so familiar to us from contemporary societies? When did this human behaviour emerge? How was it affected by and how did it affect human evolution? We argue that such souvenir practices have a long history and that, when they became routine features of early human life, they formed a cultural niche that altered selection pressures on autobiographical memory and the sense of self [6, 7]. Here “autobiographical memory” refers to episodic memory for personally experienced events and to second‐hand family narratives integrated into one's personal identity. Such memories support continuity of the sense of self over time.

section: Hypothesis for the Evolutionary Role of Souvenirs
paragraphs.text: The hypothesis is specific: personally curated keepsakes acted as external memory devices that enactively cued recall and authenticated personal pasts, memories, and experiences through direct material engagement. We suggest that the reliance on the physical (e.g., visual and haptic) and contextual characteristics of keepsakes enhanced selection pressures on neural systems for linking memories with external cues and improving source monitoring (the ability to identify if a memory came from internal thought or an external event). Our hypothesis extends existing archaeological inferences about “memory objects” and 4E (embodied, embedded, enactive, extended) philosophical accounts of extended memory [8] by making an explicit evolutionary claim. It also differs in time depth and in level of analysis: we locate the behaviour in the late Lower Palaeolithic, among ancestral rather than modern human populations, and we treat keepsakes in the first instance as tokens of a personal, individual relationship with a particular place, event, or person, rather than as vehicles of collective meaning or as markers of rank.

The “extended mind” thesis argues for active externalism and cognitive coupling between internal processes and environmental resources [9] but does not provide an evolutionary model by itself. Important exceptions ask when in hominin history material scaffolding began to matter [10] and extend a distributed account of memory and reasoning into deep time [11], but neither treats personal keepsakes or specifies a selective consequence attached to them. Our proposal focuses on personal keepsakes as the precursors of current memory aids (e.g., notebooks, photos) that effectively extend one's mind. Unlike general extended‐mind arguments, our hypothesis includes an evolutionary model, provided by niche‐construction theory and gene–culture co‐evolution, explaining how organisms modify informational environments in ways that feedback on development and selection [12, 13, 14]. Neuroimaging studies show that culturally scaffolded tool use and toolmaking training can induce plastic changes in primate and human frontoparietal networks [15, 16, 17, 18, 19], and this has been explicitly linked to gene–culture pathways in which culturally stabilized developmental demands bias long‐term selection on cognitive mechanisms [20, 21]. Our argument, which focuses on souvenirs as “memory tools,” uses extended‐memory insights to explain the cognitive function of keepsakes, and uses niche‐construction theory to specify how a stable “souvenir niche” can shape selection.

It seems that souvenir collection appeared late in the archaeological record. Throughout human prehistory, and mostly during the first 2.5 My of human biological and cultural evolution, evidence of routine possession of items bearing potential mnemonic or sentimental value is anecdotal at best (e.g., [22]). A threshold for the emergence of the “souvenir niche” could be suggested during Middle Pleistocene times, ~500 kya in specific regions of the Old World. This threshold coincides with significant biological and cultural transformations related to the replacement of Homo erectus by Neanderthals, Denisovans and/or Homo sapiens and the termination of a long and successful mode of adaptation, the Acheulean cultural complex of the Lower Palaeolithic period [23, 24, 25].

Our starting point is behavioural: regardless of motive, the record shows systematic collection and retention of items curated beyond purely utilitarian needs, and this routine curation is what we call the “souvenir niche.” There are two lines of evidence supporting the presence of this niche since at least the terminal Lower Palaeolithic (~500 kya) across Africa, Europe, and Asia. First, some sites contain objects with no obvious utility, including transported marine fossils/shells [26, 27], aesthetically distinctive stones possibly collected for their appearance [28], quartz crystals [29], eagle talons likely used as pendants [30], and selected pigment (ochre) pieces, sometimes modified with deliberate marking [31]. Our work in the Levant provides two examples. At Qesem Cave, small round and colourful pebbles were intentionally brought to the cave starting 400 Kya and throughout its 200 Ky use by humans. They show no evidence of practical use and were likely valued for aesthetic, mnemonic, or sentimental reasons [32]. Similarly, at the newly identified Acheulean landscape of Sakhnin Valley, Lower Galilee, Israel, about ten of over 200 surveyed handaxes were shaped around fossil imprints or geological features in the flint nodule, retained at the centre of the face where they can be seen and touched (Figure 3 [33]). Such nodules are harder to knap and were avoided in ordinary handaxe production. Their features are diagnostic of the valley's fossil‐ and geode‐rich outcrops, thus tying the objects to a specific locale.

Second, some sites contain artefacts that were made and used earlier than the deposits in which they were found and show little evidence of intensive secondary use, suggesting they were curated rather than simply recycled. The recycling of old patinated items frequently involved exploiting them as materials from which new items were produced. However, analyses of double‐patinated flint artefacts from the Late Acheulean sites of Revadim and Jaljulia and from post‐Acheulean Qesem Cave emphasize an additional, distinct practice (Figures 1, 2). This latter trajectory involves the systematic collection of older tools and selective, minimal edge reshaping (small removals to refresh or shape a cutting edge) that preserves earlier “old” patinated surfaces and visible scars, that is, the artefacts' earlier “biographies” [35]; but these patinas imply an interval long enough that such items were re‐encountered in the landscape rather than handed on. Wear traces visible under magnification indicate that their second phase of use was generally light, consistent with curation as keepsakes or souvenirs [36]. Building on this, the authors interpret these pieces as “memory objects,” emphasizing that the working edge was refreshed without removing the older surfaces, so earlier traces remain visually prominent [34, 36]. They further argue that this pattern is unlikely to reflect raw‐material scarcity or a least‐effort strategy, because fresh tools dominate the assemblage, yet recycled pieces repeatedly retain the older surfaces rather than being fully reworked [34, 37]. Related work similarly interprets the collection and recycling of patinated scrapers as attention to object itineraries, explicitly framing them in mnemonic terms: In this context, Efrati [37] suggests that the distinct visual and tactile contrast of the double patina effect (where fresh reduction sequences are juxtaposed against older, weathered surfaces) afforded an enactive perceptual experience. By preserving these old colourful layers, the recycled artifacts may have served as tangible extensions of their source locations and past histories, including with particular individuals, thereby helping to physically authenticate memories through direct material engagement.

These accounts establish that Middle Pleistocene humans systematically curated old artifacts, special stones, and specific geological features for reasons partly independent of their immediate function, and that mnemonic roles are archaeologically plausible [33, 37, 38]. Empirically, these behaviours are inferred from repeated patterns of transport, long‐term retention, and deposition of items with little or no clear utilitarian advantage. For example, manuports and fossils carried far from their geological sources, and curated “heirloom” pieces showing long use‐lives and episodic reworking rather than single‐use discard. Such patterned curation across multiple contexts is difficult to explain by immediate functional needs alone but is consistent with keeping objects as durable prompts for remembering places, events, or people. As an interpretive analogue, later prehistoric research argues that some “cached” or deliberately deposited objects—including mundane household items—can be understood as emotionally charged and entwined with personal identities and continuing bonds, often retained for a time and then disposed of in culturally appropriate ways [39]. Notably, Kissel and Fuentes [40] have asked how Pleistocene objects “were able to mean something” for early humans, focusing on the ability to make objects intended to produce a response in the mind of another. Here, we extend the question to objects collected to evoke a memory in the mind of one's future self. Such keepsakes “were able to mean something” as indexes, rather than symbols—by their real connection to a past person, place, or event—and thus require no conventional symbolic meaning.

Comparable mnemonic interpretations have also been proposed for later prehistory [38]. In the Neolithic, personal ornaments are sometimes interpreted as curated heirlooms (a subtype of keepsake) that can carry memories of owners and makers and help maintain a perceived presence of the dead in the lives of the living [41]. Heirlooms may also have had broader social consequences: they could materialize links to an ancestral past and help legitimate identities, rank, and claims to resources, particularly in early chiefdom contexts, with examples from Late Neolithic Iberian polished stone toolheads and inscribed vessels in Zhou‐period China to Māori heirlooms linked by form and oral tradition to Eastern Polynesian origins [42]. A different form of keepsake is suggested in later prehistoric Britain (c. 2500–600 BC), where human remains were curated for multiple generations and then redeposited in settlements or graves, consistent with keepsakes linked to remembered individuals [43]. Such behaviours are also documented in contemporary Indigenous societies, where certain artefacts are termed “pieces of places” or “gifts of the ancestors” and serve to preserve memories and experiences tied to meaningful locations, often related to ancestors or to the creation of stories and myths [44, 45, 46]. Fossils were curated in much the same way, with sub‐Saharan African non‐western societies transporting fossil manuports away from their source outcrops, including a Stegodon molar at Ishango, DR Congo (~21 kya) and a trilobite carried ~10 km into a Later Stone Age shelter in the Cederberg, South Africa [47]. Relatedly, ethnographic research on intra‐African mobility describes “memory objects” as personal items that elicit memories of home, significant places, and social relations [48].

Humans occupied the Levant for at least 1.5 My, so one might wonder why this behaviour only emerged at ~500 kya. We suggest an ecological explanation: prey body size in the Levant declined through the Pleistocene [49, 50], and the elephant, a stable and high‐return resource, disappeared around 400 kya, alongside the demise of H. erectus and the end of the Acheulean [23, 51]. Hunting smaller, evasive, and more numerous prey demanded development of new methods and expansion to new territories, and this was likely experienced by hunter‐gatherers as rupture rather than adjustment [52]. It was met not only by re‐planning foraging but also by rebuilding one's relationship to the land through story, myth, and detailed ecological knowledge [52, 53]. We propose that once a dependable relationship to particular places could no longer be taken for granted, portable pieces of those places and/or of the new hunting territories [54] became worth keeping, each tied to one person's own experience of the place rather than to the group's. This, rather than navigation, is what we mean by “place‐based obligations” and “access to places”: claims that follow from a remembered personal connection to a locale [55, 56, 57]. We would therefore expect the practice to track megaherbivore decline in space and time, rather than precede it.

Philosophical and cognitive‐science research suggests that autobiographical memory is often distributed across persons and things: “evocative objects” can cue, scaffold, or partly constitute personal memories, enabling more reliable and detailed recall [58, 59, 60]. From an interaction‐based perspective, such objects can be considered as facilitating a mnemonic experience. We use this term in the standard sense of episodic recollection: retrieval of the what–where–when of a particular past event, accompanied by autonoetic awareness, the sense of re‐experiencing one's own past, or “mental time travel” [61, 62]. What keepsakes add is that such recollection is an effortful, active search ([63], 21–44) that is cued and sustained by multisensory engagement with the object itself, by seeing, holding and handling a thing that was present at the remembered event [64]. Our concern in what follows is not the architecture of episodic memory as such, but what it meant to collect and keep such objects in the Lower Palaeolithic, and how it might have facilitated such memories.

Most discussions, however, focus on general cognitive scaffolds (e.g., notebooks, photos, calendars) or on group‐level symbolic systems (e.g., numerical notation systems, writing, calendrical devices, and mapping systems), and they rarely distinguish the special role of personal keepsakes. For example, some suggest that European Upper Palaeolithic cave art acted as knowledge transmission systems and/or decoded astronomical/celestial information [65]. In other cases, Palaeolithic engravings and depictions were suggested to stand for early maps, intended to preserve knowledge about the landscape [66].

Souvenirs differ on four dimensions. First, episodic specificity: they are often indexically tied to a concrete person–place–event, supplying high‐diagnostic cues for hippocampal pattern completion [67]. This tie is material, not conventional: patina colour indexes the locality an “old” flint item came from (Figures 1, 2), fossil or geode inclusions index the outcrop a flint nodule came from (Figure 3). A keepsake need not be a non‐utilitarian object: the pieces in Figure 3 are handaxes, but the feature that indexes their source has no functional role and was costly to retain. Second, authentication: because episodic memory is reconstructive and prone to error, keepsakes serve as more than recall cues—they provide external perceptual and contextual detail supporting attribution of a recollection to perception rather than imagination. In source‐monitoring terms [68], a material token strengthens perceptual and contextual features that help distinguish real experiences from imagination. We use “authentication” throughout in this minimal sense: a keepsake cannot by itself certify that a given recollection is veridical. What it does is narrow the space of plausible sources. Mahr and Csibra [69] stress a social version of this function, in which remembering an event lets a person assert it to others and be held responsible for that assertion; our claim is narrower, that the object serves its keeper as evidence that the memory represents a genuine event that happened. Third, intentional investment: acquiring, transporting, and maintaining a keepsake requires time, effort, and attention, effectively committing cognitive and material resources to make a particular episode memorable and to anchor it to an external, stable object. Fourth, personal reference: a keepsake's meaning is indexical and private rather than conventional and shared, so it need not be legible to anyone but its keeper. Objects can of course combine these roles: an heirloom may be both a personal keepsake and a public claim. But the mnemonic function we describe does not require an audience. Together, these features make keepsakes a distinctive class of mnemonic aid with potential fitness payoffs for social coordination when obligations, alliance histories, or claims to particular places depend on credible personal memory. Keepsakes are also affectively charged, and objects reliably at hand scaffold the regulation of emotion and mood as well as remembering [70, 71]; affective salience is plausibly what made curation persistent enough to become routine.

section: Souvenir‐Keeping Is Likely Unique to Humans
paragraphs.text: Non‐human mammals and birds do not keep souvenirs in the human sense. They may use physical landmarks as memory aids (e.g., the big tree near the river), but object collection is tied to function. Previous claims to the contrary have later proved false. For example, the “magpie shiny thing” trope is a European cultural stereotype suggesting that Eurasian magpies (Pica pica) are attracted to shiny objects and collect them. However, a study of wild magpies found no evidence of attraction; instead, birds were wary of metallic objects [72]. Other examples come from corvids that manage and cache objects for food security and tool safekeeping [73, 74, 75], or bowerbird males, who amass decorations as extended sexual displays to attract females for mating [76]. Claims about dogs burying toys and cats “collecting” corpses also reduce to caching and provisioning: food hoarding across mammals is a widespread foraging adaptation, not memento keeping [77]. Pet cats return only a minority of kills to households, consistent with central‐place transport or owner provisioning rather than collecting souvenirs [78]. Woodrats (packrats) build refuse‐and‐nest middens that incidentally archive materials but serve ecological and architectural functions, not memory preservation [79]. Across these cases, collected items serve sexual displays, cache protection, or den construction. Two experimental studies show that captive great apes are attracted to odd, shiny objects (orangutans) and crystals (chimpanzees), but neither study demonstrated preservation of these objects as mementos of a particular place or event [80, 81]: the chimpanzees even preserved a large crystal in their dormitory for 2 days before returning it in exchange for food, which demonstrates sustained interest in an unusual object but not curation tied to a remembered episode. Similarly, an experiment with stone‐handling Japanese macaques (Macaca fuscata) showed that they prefer stones and places where others had already handled stones, suggesting these places are “play stations” [82].

section: Souvenir‐Keeping Is Likely Unique to Humans
paragraphs.text: None of these behaviours entails retaining items as mnemonic keepsakes or demonstrates collection of objects as personal, beyond functional, mementos. Behaviourally, a souvenir would be identified by different criteria: an individual keeps one particular object safe over a long period, neither discarding it nor trading it for food, and returns to engage with it from time to time, in ways specific to that object and individual. Such a pattern may exist but go unobserved, as detecting it requires following a known individual and a known object over months.

Autobiographical memory depends on binding items to contexts and on reconstructive retrieval. According to a three‐component model of medial temporal lobe function, the hippocampus supports pattern completion, reinstating full episodes from partial cues; the perirhinal cortex provides familiarity signals; and the parahippocampal cortex contributes contextual information [83, 84, 85]. When recollection is vivid and detailed, it further recruits a broader cortical network, including the angular gyrus and posterior cingulate cortex that integrate these elements into a consciously experienced memory [86, 87]. Keepsakes operate as high‐diagnostic retrieval cues that increase the probability of successful pattern completion for person–place–object bindings. They also support source monitoring—the evaluative processes that attribute memories to internal or external origins—by increasing available sensory detail and contextual coherence [68, 88]. Lateral and anterior prefrontal regions implicated in source monitoring can use the additional external evidence to reduce false recall.

Repeated use of keepsakes, supported by social practices that value them, directs attention to links between people, places, and objects [89]. This process parallels the way adult‐child conversations about past events scaffold the development of autobiographical memory by providing linguistic and cultural structure [90, 91]. We do not posit a dedicated mechanism for combining internal and external memory, but two abilities that can be measured and that differ between people: telling remembered from imagined events [92, 93], and judging when to rely on memory rather than on an external token [94]. Such differences are partly heritable [95], which is what selection requires. In populations where keepsakes are routine, individuals who are better at integrating internal traces with external tokens and at monitoring sources will perform better in credibility‐sensitive tasks, like maintaining alliances and tracking reciprocity. Source memory, rather than recognition memory, is selectively enhanced for the faces of cheaters [96], individuals with better source memory cooperate more with cooperators and less with cheaters [97], and ordinary memory errors are large enough to constrain which reciprocity strategies can be sustained [98].

The same selective logic, that accurate evaluation of the content and source of one's own information is advantageous, has been proposed for a later, language‐driven setting [99]. In this cultural niche, the ability to use keepsakes to support autobiographical memory would be beneficial for the organism, and therefore its underlying neural mechanisms should be favoured by natural selection. Neural plasticity data show that tool‐use and toolmaking training can induce lasting structural changes in primate and human frontoparietal networks [17, 19]. Such plasticity has been proposed as a mechanism through which culturally stabilized tool use may create a consistent developmental demand and thereby selection pressures over evolutionary timescales [20, 21]. Indeed, culture and technology can shape genetic evolution of cognition by favouring inherited changes that make the underlying learning and performance processes more efficient, a route often discussed under the “Baldwin effect” [12, 13, 100]. Exogram theories offer a longer‐term perspective: as external memory tools multiplied, they changed how people used memory and reshaped brain organization ([101]; see [102], on the subsequent interdisciplinary debate). We propose that a similar process might have taken place for souvenirs, where coevolutionary dynamics between external memory practices and neural organization facilitated the development of autobiographical memory and the sense of self.

Why is this hypothesis new? Three bodies of work set the stage for our proposal, though each falls short of fully explaining this phenomenon. First, Lower–Middle Pleistocene archaeology has offered specific cases of curated artefacts interpreted as mnemonic or biographical objects [34, 36], without inquiring further into their psychological and evolutionary meaning. Second, the philosophy and psychology of extended and distributed memory have analysed how objects couple to autobiographical remembering, often highlighting how active, embodied engagement with material affordances scaffolds personal recall, and often with respect to modern aids, but generally without evolutionary claims [58, 59, 60]. Material engagement theory develops this line furthest and has placed memory and the self at its centre, treating remembering as enacted through and with things rather than merely cued by them [6, 103, 104]. Extended memory research has shown how many artifacts—from notebooks to digital devices—integrate with memory, yet rarely proposes selection consequences. Where it does reach into deep time [10, 11], the focus is on scaffolding for skill, social learning and collective intelligence rather than on personal mnemonic objects. Third, niche construction and scaffolded cognition accounts treat language, numeracy, notation systems, and tool repertoires as drivers of evolutionary change [13, 100, 105, 106], but have not directly addressed souvenirs. Closest to our own hypothesis, Jablonka [99] argues that autobiographical memory evolved culturally to counter the false memories and deceit that language made possible in large, differentiated groups. We complement this proposal by highlighting a material driver at a considerably earlier time period.

Our proposal bridges over these approaches to close the abovementioned gaps by focusing on souvenirs as a particular class of external cue and providing an evolutionary account for their importance in psychological development. People, places, and public objects such as rock art could already cue memory in prehistory, but they were fixed in place and publicly shared. Kelly [107] surveys many such devices, almost always for transmitting shared knowledge rather than personal episodes, and her corpus could be re‐examined for the personal use we propose. Souvenirs made such reminders portable and added a durable material trace that could help check and communicate the source of self‐relevant episodes. We therefore propose that routine souvenir practices created a cultural niche that strengthened selection on source monitoring and the integration of people‐place‐event details. This is consistent with evidence that sustained training can remodel neural systems through plasticity, as shown for tool‐use learning in macaques and stone‐toolmaking training in humans [17, 19]. Selection need not be for ‘better memory in general,’ but for better use of external traces, such as by cognitive mechanisms that integrate internal recollection with these traces to weigh memories by reliability in credibility‐sensitive tasks.

Our contribution is threefold. First, time depth: earlier discussions of object curation, shared cultural meaning, and object‐mediated status concentrate on the Upper Palaeolithic and later, and on modern humans; we locate the behaviour in the late Lower Palaeolithic, among our Middle Pleistocene ancestors. Second, level of analysis: rather than viewing curated objects as carriers of collective meaning or as markers of rank, we treat them as tokens of an individual's own relationship with a place, event, or person. Personal and social functions are not mutually exclusive, and could have developed independently, at different orders. We emphasize the personal level because it relies on a simpler assumption: an object that indexes its owner's past requires no shared convention, no agreed meaning, and no audience, whereas heirlooms, legitimation, and authentication before others presuppose all three. Third, evolutionary consequence: we propose that once routine, this behavioural pattern might have fed back on selection for source monitoring and for the integration of person–place–event detail, thereby facilitating the evolution of autobiographical memory and the sense of self. What we share with earlier workers is the observation that non‐utilitarian curation is real and that mnemonic readings of it are plausible; what is original is the conjunction of these three claims.

section: Counter‐Arguments and How to Test the Hypothesis
paragraphs.text: Multiple alternative explanations can be suggested. Non‐instrumental collecting may be explained by aesthetics per se, raw‐material caching, or craft practice. The authentication function might be achieved solely by language. Yet one can arbitrate between these explanations by testing the discriminating predictions of our hypothesis. If keepsakes served episodic memory and authentication, we expect deliberate preservation of prior surfaces and minimal reworking that retains visible biographies, as documented at several Lower Palaeolithic sites in Israel [35, 108] and beyond [109, 110, 111, 112], coupled with spatial associations to life‐history loci (e.g., dwelling areas, hearths, recurrent occupation layers) rather than only raw‐material caches. We further expect items with no functional role at all, such as fossils, crystals and colourful pebbles, and retention of features that make an item harder to produce or to use (Figure 3). If selection is mnemonic rather than economic, raw‐material availability should not predict souvenir density, and source, raw material and patina type should be more diverse than local procurement would yield (Figures 1, 2).

section: Counter‐Arguments and How to Test the Hypothesis
paragraphs.text: No single one of these is decisive, and the weakest is wear. Use‑wear may frequently reflect handling and light tasks; however, evidence of functional optimisation does not negate a mnemonic role, as actively integrating a curated item into daily tasks can further embed it within personal and cultural narratives [36, 37]. The hypothesis therefore fails on the conjunction rather than on any single criterion, that is, on assemblages of curated items that are functionally optimised, locally sourced and undifferentiated in provenance. At a cognitive level, communities that valorise keepsakes should exhibit stronger source‐memory accuracy for self‐relevant events, controlling for narrative scaffolds, and heavier use of external cues in memory justification.

section: Counter‐Arguments and How to Test the Hypothesis
paragraphs.text: The burden of proof is thus empirical. Archaeology can combine microwear/residue analysis and micro‐polish with patina stratigraphy to test whether putative keepsakes show deliberate retention of older patinated surfaces with minimal edge‐refresh and wear consistent with repeated handling/light tasks (rather than task‐optimized cutting or chopping). It can also point at more potential items as souvenirs, such as grave goods like the extraordinary handaxe deposited together with pre‐Neanderthals at the Sima de los Huesos site in Spain [113]; handaxes shaped around fossils or special geological phenomena [33]; the collection of geodes, fossils and special stones [53, 114] or specific animal body parts [115]. Spatial statistics can then test whether these curated items are non‐randomly associated with domestic or commemorative contexts—especially hearths and recurrent occupation levels—rather than only knapping floors or raw‐material caches. Cross‐cultural work can test whether keepsakes are disproportionately used as memory verification tools in credibility‐sensitive domains amongst past and contemporary indigenous groups, as well as modern societies. Developmental studies can test whether early caregiver–child token practices increase attention to person–place–object bindings and improve later source monitoring. Agent‐based models can assess whether token‐supported memory credibility increases coalition stability and cooperation sufficiently to produce selection for parameters that enhance cue integration and monitoring. None of these tests presupposes the conclusion; they do specify how the hypothesis could be wrong.

section: Implications for Anthropology and Human Evolution
paragraphs.text: If supported, the hypothesis shifts how we interpret artefact collecting beyond the purely “functional” realm in human evolutionary history. Curated pieces become not just aesthetically or symbolically significant but serve as proto‐technologies in the service of the autobiographical self. Anthropologically, this suggests that durable keepsakes could have reinforced existing senses of identity by providing material anchors for personal narratives, relationships, and obligations [56, 57]. Socially, it links material culture to how credibility is earned, displayed, and assessed in small‐scale societies, where proof of one's personal past affects alliance maintenance, gift exchange, and access to places [55]. Evolutionarily, the hypothesis adds an autobiographical strand to existing narratives about language, symbol systems, and material engagement as drivers of cognitive change [103]. It frames autobiographical memory as emerging within a niche that is not only social but also technological and material. If token‐guided retrieval and source‐checking improve performance in credibility‐sensitive social tasks, then routine engagement with keepsakes could, over long timescales, select for neural mechanisms that bind episodic detail to external cues and evaluate their provenance—consistent with evidence for neural plasticity [17, 19] and gene–culture dynamics. This perspective treats the broadly shared practice of personal keepsakes as an evolutionary grounded mechanism for scaffolding and narrating the autobiographical self rather than a recent cultural phenomenon [55, 57, 116].

section: Implications for Anthropology and Human Evolution
paragraphs.text: We emphasize scope. The claim is not that keepsakes alone gave rise to the self or autobiographical memory, nor that all curated artefacts are mnemonic. We also do not deny that keepsakes can serve a social function wherever they can be observed by others; we emphasize the personal only because it assumes the least, operating without shared conventions or an audience. Rather, where and when souvenir practices became routine and normative (possibly later than the earliest examples in the archaeological record), they provided reliable material support for two functions that were already useful in social life: reminding individuals of past episodes, and making those episodes easier to validate, privately or to others, by linking them to a durable trace. By stabilizing recall and enabling source‐checking, such practices could have strengthened selection for skills in remembering events and evaluating their provenance. This is a narrow but tractable evolutionary pathway, compatible with other drivers. Jablonka [99] and Sutton [117] also examined the evolution of autobiographical memory and source monitoring, but locate the pressure in language, larger groups, and delayed‐return economies, once shared experience no longer corrected individual memory. Ours is a material driver, set off by an ecological disruption that preceded all three.

Three lines of work can advance or falsify the proposal. First, targeted reanalysis of Lower–Middle Pleistocene assemblages that already contain candidate souvenir items should include systematic tests for authentication. For example, candidate keepsake items among reworked patinated artefacts are expected to show consistent patterning, including selective retention of earlier surfaces, minimal edge reshaping that preserves biographies, and occurrence in repeatedly used sites or layers (reoccupation contexts). Second, behavioural experiments can test key predictions by measuring whether personal keepsakes improve autobiographical recall, source monitoring, and credibility in cooperation tasks (e.g., partner choice, reciprocity tracking) compared with matched controls without keepsakes. Third, longitudinal training studies can test a neurobiological prediction: learning to use keepsakes to support recall and source monitoring should induce measurable neural plasticity, analogous to the effects of tool‐use and toolmaking training [17, 19]. Nowadays, there is no doubt that memory serves both individual and social purposes, and that contemporary memory tools amplify these functions. If curated keepsakes are the precursors of such tools, we should be able to see their traces both in stones and in minds.
